history: Café came to France from the Ottoman world. The Arabic word is qahwa. Turkish made it kahve, and the TLFi says French took it either straight from Turkish or through Italian, where Venice had caffè in 1615. French writers spelt the strange new word in many ways: caoua in 1592, in a Latin text, and cauueh or cafeh in 1651. The drink quickly gave its name to the place where it was served. The sources quoted by the TLFi date the first café in Marseille to 1654, and in 1672 an Armenian called Pascal opened one at the Saint-Germain fair in Paris. Today un café is both: you order un café au café. In France, plain café means a small black coffee.
historyEinfach: Café is an Arabic word: qahwa. It came to France through Turkish, and maybe through Italian. First it was only the drink. Soon it was also the place where people drink it. The first cafés in France opened in Marseille and Paris in the 1600s. Un café in France is a small black coffee.

elsewhere.text: Turkish passed the Arabic word on to Europe, together with the drink and the coffee house.
